name: Contractbook
tagline: Contract lifecycle platform: templates, e-signing, storage, renewal tracking and data-driven contract automation.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The boring 80 percent of Contractbook is a database of contracts, a template engine with merge fields, a signing link, and a reminder before renewal dates. An agent can build that in a weekend and it will genuinely work for one freelancer or a small shop with a dozen agreements a year. The part that does not survive is the part you only care about when something goes wrong: a defensible audit trail, identity assurance on the signer, eIDAS or ESIGN posture, and the integrations that push signed contract data into HR and CRM systems. A homemade click-to-sign with a hashed PDF and an IP log is often legally sufficient for simple electronic signatures, but you are now the one arguing that in a dispute. Build it if your contracts are low stakes and you mostly want to stop losing them in email.
coreLoopDIY: Fill a markdown template with counterparty data, render a PDF, send a tokenized signing link, log the signature with a hash and timestamp, and email you before the renewal date.
requirements: SMTP credentials for signing links and reminders
A domain with HTTPS so signing links are not obviously sketchy
Offsite backups of the SQLite file, because this is now your only copy of your contracts
whatYouLose: Identity assurance and qualified signature options, so no BankID, no SMS OTP, no advanced or qualified eIDAS tiers
A tamper-evident audit trail that someone else vouches for rather than one you maintain in your own database
Native integrations that read and write contract data to HR, CRM and accounting systems
Counterparty-side polish: negotiation comments, redlining, version history that both sides can see
Someone to call when a signature is challenged or a renewal is missed
moatNotes: The legal defensibility is outsourced trust, not code. Nobody buys contract software because the templating is clever.
whyPeopleStillPay: Contracts are a low-frequency, high-consequence workflow, which is exactly the shape where people pay to not be the responsible party. A signed agreement that a court or an acquirer might inspect years from now is worth more when the audit trail lives with a vendor that has a compliance page and a support inbox. Add the integrations that keep signed data flowing into HR and CRM without manual copying, plus the fact that legal and ops teams do not want to own a self-hosted app, and the subscription is cheap relative to the perceived downside.
notes: Fine as a private contract shelf with reminders; less fine as the thing you cite in a dispute.
prompt:
Build a local-first contract manager as a single Next.js 15 app (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind). No SaaS accounts, no telemetry, no cloud services.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 + TypeScript + Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/contracts.db, migrations in ./migrations run on boot
- Playwright's bundled Chromium for HTML to PDF rendering
- nodemailer for outbound mail, SMTP config from .env only
- Single-operator auth: one bcrypt password hash in .env, signed httpOnly session cookie. No user table.

Data model:
- counterparties: name, email, company, address
- templates: title, markdown body with {{mustache}} merge fields, declared field list
- contracts: template_id, counterparty_id, title, merged_markdown snapshot, status (draft, sent, signed, declined, expired), effective_date, end_date, renewal_notice_days, value, currency, pdf_path, content_sha256
- signature_events: contract_id, actor (owner or counterparty), event type (sent, viewed, signed, declined), typed_name, ip, user_agent, iso timestamp, sha256 of the PDF at that moment

Features in scope:
1. CRUD for counterparties and templates. Template editor is a plain textarea with a live merge-field list parsed from the body.
2. "New contract from template": pick template + counterparty, form auto-generates inputs for each merge field, prefilled from counterparty data where names match.
3. Render the merged markdown to a clean A4 PDF (serif body, page numbers, signature block at the end). Store the file under ./data/pdfs and record content_sha256.
4. Send for signature: generate a 32-byte random token, email the counterparty a link at /sign/[token]. Page shows the PDF inline, requires typed full name plus an explicit "I agree to sign electronically" checkbox, then writes a signature_event and stamps a signature page onto a new PDF version. Log a view event on first load.
5. Dashboard: contracts grouped by status, plus a "renewals" panel listing anything where end_date minus renewal_notice_days is within 30 days.
6. A /api/cron/reminders route, protected by a CRON_SECRET, that emails the operator about upcoming renewals and unsigned contracts older than 7 days. Include a crontab line in the README.
7. Per-contract audit page rendering the full signature_events timeline, and a CSV export of all contracts.

Explicitly out of scope: redlining, multi-party or sequential signing, negotiation comments, CRM or HR integrations, ID verification, qualified eIDAS signatures, mobile apps.

Deliverables: working app, seed script with two templates (mutual NDA, freelance services agreement) and one demo counterparty, .env.example, and a README that states plainly that this produces a simple electronic signature with a self-maintained audit trail and is not a qualified signature service. Add a nightly script that copies data/ to a timestamped backup folder.
